Dear Administrator Oz, 
 
The Colorado Department of Health Care Policy & Financing (HCPF) serves as Coloradoâ€™s 
single state agency for the administration of Health First Colorado (Coloradoâ€™s Medicaid 
program) and Child Health Plan Plus (CHP+, which is Coloradoâ€™s Children's Health Insurance 
Program (CHIP)). We write to comment on the proposed HHS federal rule Medicare and 
Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards 
and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed 
Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies 
and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-
Facilitated Exchanges. (CMS-0062-P). Specifically, our Medicaid agency is concerned about 
CMSâ€™ proposed interoperability standards, especially as they apply to prior authorization for 
drugs, and how this proposed rule may unintentionally slow patientsâ€™ access to prescribed 
medications rather than expedite their access to needed medications.  
 
We understand that this rule builds on prior rulemaking around interoperability, access, and 
prior authorization, to expand many of those requirements to cover prior authorization for 
drugs. In that context, we write to express two main concerns: 1.The feasibility of 
implementing the provisions of this rule within the proposed timeline and as our agency is 
also currently engaged in implementing major systems and policy transformations related to 
H.R. 1, otherwise known as the Working Families Tax Credit Act (WFTC); and 2. To ask for 
clarification from CMS about specific details of drug prior authorization (PAR) timelines as 
compared to non-drug PARs and to better understand how CMSâ€™s proposed 24 hour response 
applies to PAR decisions and how decisions within that timeline may negatively impact 
patients.

1. Feasibility of CMS Implementation Timeline Given Concurrent Information 
Technology Efforts 
 
HCPF respectfully submits that CMSâ€™s proposed implementation timeline is unrealistic,  
considering that state programs are planning for updates to a new National Council for 
Prescription Drug Programs (NCPDP), ANSI-accredited standards standard and for a move to 
larger, FDA-required National Drug Code Format (NDC) format in the coming years, when 
FDA will assign new 12-digit NDCs and convert all previously assigned 10-digit NDCs to the 
uniform 12-digit NDC format.  We emphasize that this transition will be required for nearly 
all drugs, except certain biologics, to 12-digit NDCs on March 7, 2033.   
 
In addition, in the near term, to comply with CMS and federal statutory requirements, our 
agency is concurrently engaged in implementing major systems and policy transformations 
related to H.R. 1, otherwise known as the Working Families Tax Credit (WFTC) Act.  We must 
prioritize the implementation of statutory community engagement requirements by January 
1, 2027, as well as the transition to six-month renewal requirements for nearly all of our 
Medicaid members. We cannot overstate that for successful implementation of these 
requirements, and to ensure minimal disruption for our Medicaid members we will need to 
make major technical adjustments to our stateâ€™s information technology systems and ensure 
coordination with our vendors as well as communications outreach to our members. For 
many specific aspects of these systems updates we anticipate the need for additional  
CMS guidance and technical assistance, all of which will take time. We suggest that a three-
year time frame for implementation is more realistic.  
 
2. Clarifications Needed for Drug Prior Authorization (PAR) Timelines to Prevent 
Unintended Consequences for Patients 
We request that the PAR response allowance time be set at the same standard required for 
other benefits, that is 72 hours, instead of limiting PAR to 24 hours for pharmacy benefits. 
To benefit patient health, although we currently respond within 24 hours, we have seen that 
for some patients and some drugs, up to 72 hours may allow for more complete medical 
review and provider communication.  
Itâ€™s also very important for the final rule to clarify whether a response is required within 24 
hours versus a decision within 24 hours.  We offer this comment in response to CMSâ€™ specific 
request for comments related to a 24-hour timeframe for state Medicaid FFS programs and 
CHIP FFS programs, to respond to requests for prior authorization of covered outpatient 
drugs, at pages 199235-19938 of the proposed rule at the links provided. Currently, we 
provide a PAR response within the designated time frame, however the response may 
indicate that additional information is required to fulfill the requirements for approval.  This 
provides the requestor with valuable information which may lead to approval.  If a decision 
is required within 24 hours, the number of denials will increase in order to be compliant and 
appropriate therapy will be delayed.  HCPF is not staffed to support the increase in denials 
that would be caused by such a change, and it would delay care for members who

potentially will meet our requirements if a small amount of additional time is allowed for 
more complete review.   
Requiring a final decision, versus a response, within 24 hours, unintentionally and 
unfortunately, eliminates the opportunity to request specifics about the need and potential 
patient benefit from specific drugs, that have not been provided initially, and allows for the 
requester-provider to supply additional information, rather than needing to start the process 
over again as a new PAR. In sum, we believe that patients will benefit and administrative 
bottlenecks will be avoided, if CMS clarifies that 24 hour response time is preferred but that 
a 72 hour decision time frame is allowed when needed to assure informed pharmacist and 
medical decision making. An October 1, 2027 compliance date may be unfeasible for this 
portion of the rule. We suggest that CMS consider a later, separate effective date and 
consider exercising enforcement  discretion to allow adequate time for necessary IT systems 
adjustments to implement this portion of the rule.  
Conclusion    
We thank HHS for the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule. We look forward to 
continuing to work with HHS to help ensure the implementation of health information 
technology systems that successfully respond to federal statutory requirements and prior 
authorization timelines that distinguish between prompt PAR responses and PAR decisions 
that each will best support patient care.  
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
Jim Leonard, PharmD 
Deputy Director, Pharmacy Office
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Colorado Department of Health Care Policy & Financing (HCPF); signed by Jim Leonard, PharmD, Deputy Director, Pharmacy Office.
- **Stakeholder type:** Government
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Colorado single state agency for Health First Colorado (Medicaid) and Child Health Plan Plus (CHIP); pharmacy office leadership.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

HCPF is concerned that CMS's proposed implementation timeline and drug prior authorization response requirements may be unrealistic for state Medicaid/CHIP programs and could unintentionally slow access to medications. It requests a three-year implementation timeframe, a later or separate effective date with enforcement discretion for IT changes, and clarification that a 24-hour pharmacy PA response may request additional information while a final decision may occur within 72 hours when needed for informed review.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE/GENERAL; STATE-EXTENSION-PROCESS indirectly.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P; proposed rule pages 19935-19938 referenced by page range; no CFR section cited.
- **Standards referenced:** NCPDP standards; National Drug Code (NDC) transition to 12-digit format; pharmacy prior authorization response/decision process.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Implementation feasibility**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** States are facing concurrent IT and policy transformations, including WFTC-related Medicaid changes and future NDC format changes.
- **Specific request:** Replace the proposed timeline with a more realistic three-year implementation timeframe.

**Topic 2: Competing state system priorities**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Clarify/Modify
- **Rationale:** Colorado must implement community engagement requirements by January 1, 2027, six-month renewals, vendor coordination, member communications, and systems changes.
- **Specific request:** CMS should provide guidance and technical assistance and account for state implementation capacity.

**Topic 3: 24-hour response vs decision**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Clarify/Modify
- **Rationale:** A final decision within 24 hours may force denials when additional clinical information could support approval.
- **Specific request:** Clarify that a 24-hour response may request more information, with a 72-hour decision timeframe when needed for informed pharmacist and medical review.

**Topic 4: Effective date and enforcement discretion**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** October 1, 2027 may be infeasible for this portion of the rule given IT systems adjustments.
- **Specific request:** Consider a later separate effective date and enforcement discretion.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S19:** HCPF addresses state readiness and explains that concurrent state/federal requirements and IT changes make the proposed timeline unrealistic.
- **S20:** HCPF directly responds to the 24-hour Medicaid/CHIP drug PA timeframe, requesting clarification between a response and final decision.
- **S22:** HCPF references NCPDP and NDC-related system work as implementation burdens, though it does not provide a cost estimate.
- **S36/S38:** HCPF's request for a three-year timeframe, separate effective date, and enforcement discretion relates to state extension/timing criteria.
- **S43:** HCPF recommends 72 hours for pharmacy benefit PAR decisions, aligned with other benefits when additional review is needed.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Adopt a three-year implementation timeframe for affected state systems.
2. Account for concurrent WFTC-related Medicaid eligibility and renewal system changes.
3. Provide CMS guidance and technical assistance for implementation.
4. Clarify that 24 hours may mean a response, not necessarily a final decision.
5. Allow a 72-hour decision timeframe when additional clinical information or review is needed.
6. Consider a later, separate effective date for drug PA timeline requirements.
7. Exercise enforcement discretion during necessary IT systems adjustments.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Unrealistic timeline, concurrent statutory IT work, NCPDP/NDC transitions, ambiguity between response and decision, increased denials, and staffing constraints.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Slower medication access, unnecessary denials, delayed care, administrative bottlenecks, and member disruption.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** State IT changes, vendor coordination, member outreach, community engagement implementation, six-month renewals, future 12-digit NDC conversion, and need for CMS guidance.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** FDA-required 12-digit NDC transition effective March 7, 2033; community engagement requirements by January 1, 2027; current Colorado practice responds within 24 hours.
- **Studies or research referenced:** None.
- **Examples provided:** Requests requiring additional information before approval; staffing impact if forced final decisions increase denials.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Colorado Medicaid and CHIP members, HCPF, state vendors, providers/requesters, pharmacists/medical reviewers, CMS.
- **Economic implications:** Major state IT and vendor coordination costs implied; increased denials would require additional staffing and administrative handling.
- **Technical feasibility:** HCPF argues the proposed October 1, 2027 date is infeasible given concurrent systems changes.
- **Patient care impact:** Final decisions forced too quickly may cause avoidable denials and delayed appropriate therapy.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Concerned; requests modification and clarification
- **Tone:** Professional, operational, cautionary
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "CMS's proposed implementation timeline is unrealistic." - Context: State feasibility concern.
2. "We request that the PAR response allowance time be set at the same standard required for other benefits, that is 72 hours." - Context: Timeframe recommendation.
3. "If a decision is required within 24 hours, the number of denials will increase." - Context: Warning about unintended consequences.
4. "A 24 hour response time is preferred but that a 72 hour decision time frame is allowed when needed." - Context: Requested clarification.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Central concern is timeline feasibility and effective dates.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - State IT, staffing, vendor, and outreach burdens are emphasized.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - HCPF questions feasibility amid NCPDP/NDC and state system changes.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Warns that rapid final decisions may increase denials and delay care.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Requires CMS, state agency, vendors, providers, and members to coordinate.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Distinguishes current PAR response workflows from final decision processes.
- [x] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Not a small payer, but raises state-program capacity constraints similar to resource-limited implementation concerns.
